swiderian: Hunter-gatherers of the plains between the Oder and the Dnieper; more than a thousand sites are known. Main spread c. 10,500–9500 BC. In Polesia, on the Neman and the upper Dnieper some researchers distinguish the related Krasnoselye culture (Lyngby tradition).
ahrensburg: Reindeer hunters of the Younger Dryas cold spell, c. 10,950–9750 BC. They also lived on lands now under the North and Baltic seas (Doggerland); isolated finds are known as far as the Orkney Islands. In Britain finds are rare (Flixton and Sewell's Cave in Yorkshire): few people lived there during the Younger Dryas. They also hunted in the hills further south: Hohler Stein (Sauerland) and Kartstein (Eifel), c. 10,100–9800 BC, and Remouchamps cave in the Belgian Ardennes.
azilian: Epipalaeolithic hunter-gatherers known for their painted pebbles. North of the Garonne the Laborian replaces them by this time.
laborian: Drawn only where dated sites are known (valleys of the Dordogne, Lot and middle Garonne). Sites south of the Garonne belong to its later stage, after 10,000 BC.
natufian: Settled foragers who harvested wild cereals with sickles and hunted gazelle. Farming will appear here around 9500 BC.
upper-tigris: Known site: Körtik Tepe (from c. 10,700 BC). Hallan Çemi and Göbekli Tepe appear later, c. 9700–9500 BC; farming here begins c. 9500–8500 BC.
zarzian: Hunter-gatherers of the Zagros Mountains (caves of Zarzi, Palegawra and Shanidar). A spread to Gobustan (Azerbaijan) and eastern Iran is suggested, but not shown here.
iberomaurusian: Hunter-gatherers of the Maghreb, known above all from the burials in Taforalt cave. In Libya (Haua Fteah cave) the same industry is called the Eastern Oranian.
agate-basin: Bison hunters of the Great Plains, an early part of the Plano tradition. About 10,500–9500 BC by the classic chronology; dated less precisely than Folsom. Towards the end of the period — the Hell Gap complex (c. 10,500–9,500 radiocarbon years ago in Holliday's summary).
eburran: The map date falls at the end of phase 1 of this industry; presence exactly in 10,000 BC is not proven.
iron-gates: Early stage: camps in caves and rock shelters. Riverside villages such as Lepenski Vir appear after 7600 BC.
osipovka: Hunter-gatherers of the Lower Amur who made some of the oldest pottery in the world, c. 14,250–8750 BC.
gromatukha: Hunter-gatherers of the Zeya valley with early pottery. Its later stage, c. 10,000–8250 BC, starts right at the date of this map.
ustinovka: Final Palaeolithic of eastern Primorye; salmon fishing and hunting. The culture spans 16,000–9000 years ago, but no site has a direct date around 10,000 BC.
sumnagin: Mesolithic hunters of Yakutia, c. 11,050–5050 BC, successors of the Dyuktai culture. Shown where the early sites are (Aldan and Middle Lena); later it spread as far as Taimyr and Chukotka.
ust-karenga: Early pottery of the upper Vitim. The earliest radiocarbon dates are disputed; luminescence dating of the sherds confirms an Ice Age start and a long pottery phase.
ushki: Hunters' camps on Ushki Lake (layer VI, dated c. 13,100–10,000 years ago at different sites) and at Anavgai 2 in central Kamchatka (c. 13,000 and c. 11,500 years ago).
epigravettian: Last Ice Age hunter-gatherers of Italy and Sicily (Riparo Tagliente, Grotta Romanelli, Addaura, Levanzo). Replaced by the Mesolithic c. 9500–9000 BC. In central and southern Italy and in Sicily the tradition continued into the early Holocene.
trialetian: Hunter-gatherers of the Caucasus; the Kmlo-2 site in Armenia dates to 11,000–10,000 BC. Caspian sites in Iran and Turkmenistan (Belt and Hotu caves) are sometimes assigned to it, but this is disputed, so Hotu and Belt are shown as a separate zone.
anetovka: Late Palaeolithic bison hunters of the Steppe Bug region. The culture spans 22,000–10,000 years ago, but no site has a direct date around 10,000 BC.
nanzhuangtou: Known from the Nanzhuangtou site, c. 10,650–9350 BC: early pottery and possibly the earliest use of millet.
zengpiyan: Known from Zengpiyan cave near Guilin, settled from c. 10,000 BC, right at the date of this map; very early pottery.
uninhabited-antarctica: No human has lived in Antarctica; it was first sighted in 1820.
uninhabited-greenland: First people arrive c. 2500 BC (Saqqaq culture).
uninhabited-north-atlantic: Faroe Islands settled c. 6th–9th century AD, Iceland in the 870s; Svalbard and Franz Josef Land discovered in 1596 and 1873. Jan Mayen was found uninhabited in the early 17th century.
uninhabited-caribbean: First settlers reach the islands c. 5000–4000 BC (Trinidad, then joined to South America, is not included).
uninhabited-remote-oceania: Settled from c. 1500 BC (Marianas, Lapita culture in Vanuatu, Fiji, Tonga, Samoa) to c. 1000–1300 AD (Hawaii, Easter Island, New Zealand). Polynesians reached Norfolk, the Chatham and the Auckland Islands only in the 13th–15th centuries AD; Campbell and Macquarie were found uninhabited in 1810. Lord Howe and the Coral Sea banks (Chesterfield, Bellona, Kenn, Marion and others) knew no people either before or after they were flooded — they were found uninhabited.
uninhabited-atlantic-islands: Canary Islands settled in the 1st millennium BC; Azores, Madeira and Cape Verde only in the 15th century AD; Bermuda and the Falklands even later. Saint Helena, Ascension, Tristan da Cunha, Sao Tome and Principe, Fernando de Noronha and South Georgia were found empty by Europeans in the 15th–18th centuries.
uninhabited-indian-ocean: Comoros settled c. 6th–8th century AD; Mascarenes, Seychelles and Chagos only in the 17th–18th centuries. The shoals that were then above water (Saya de Malha, Nazareth, Leven Bank) were never reached by anyone either. Kerguelen, Crozet, Heard and Christmas Island were found uninhabited in the 17th–19th centuries.
uninhabited-galapagos: Discovered in 1535; first permanent settlers in 1832. The Juan Fernández Islands were found uninhabited in 1574.
uninhabited-mediterranean: First settlers: Malta c. 5900 BC, Balearic Islands c. 2300 BC.
uninhabited-eastern-sahara: Hyper-arid desert during the Younger Dryas: between 20,000 and 8500 BC there were no settlements here outside the Nile valley (Kuper & Kröpelin, 2006). People came with the rains c. 8500 BC.
uninhabited-ice: Covered by an ice sheet (outline approximate, c. 12,000 years ago). The land was settled step by step as the ice melted over the following millennia.
robberg-oakhurst: Hunter-gatherers of southern Africa. The map date falls on the change from the Robberg industry (c. 18,000–12,000 years ago) to the Oakhurst industry (c. 12,000–7,000 years ago). Ancient DNA from Oakhurst rockshelter (oldest c. 10,000 years) links them to the ancestors of today's southern San. 'Khoisan' is a modern collective name, so it is not used here.
hora: Known from the Hora 1 rockshelter, used c. 21,000–8,000 years ago, with burials c. 16,000–14,000 and 9,000–8,000 years ago. No direct date at 10,000 BC.
kuumbi: Zanzibar was still part of the mainland. Occupation phase c. 13,000–11,000 years ago (dates approximate): quartz microliths, bone points, hunting and seafood. The sea cut Zanzibar off c. 9,000–8,000 years ago, and the cave was abandoned.
iwo-eleru: Rockshelter in the forest of south-western Nigeria: a burial from the end of the Ice Age (c. 13,000 years ago) and early use of canarium nuts (c. 11,300 years ago).
bosumpra: Forest-edge hunter-gatherers. The first people came c. 10,500 BC and kept using the cave in the early Holocene. No direct date at 10,000 BC.
senegal-late-msa: Here people kept making Middle Stone Age tools until c. 11,000 years ago — about 20,000 years longer than elsewhere in Africa. Ndiayène Pendao is dated c. 11,600 years ago (about 400 years after the map date); Saxomununya on the Falémé is younger than c. 11,100 years.
matupi: Layers with Later Stone Age microliths run without a visible break from over 40,000 to c. 3,000 years ago (excavations of the 1970s). No direct date at 10,000 BC.
mesa: Hunters of the Brooks Range and north-western Alaska. Mesa site: most dates c. 12,400–11,100 years ago; fluted points at Serpentine Hot Springs and Raven Bluff c. 12,000 years ago. Their spear points resemble Agate Basin points of the Great Plains.
central-alaska: Hunters of bison, wapiti and waterfowl: Broken Mammoth, Swan Point, Dry Creek, Teklanika West (c. 12,100–11,400 years ago). Microblades of the Denali type and Chindadn points. Nearby, at Upward Sun River, children were buried c. 11,500 years ago.
haida-gwaii: With the sea lower, Haida Gwaii had a broad coastal plain. Gaadu Din 2 cave was a hunting camp c. 12,500–10,700 years ago; spear points in nearby caves are over 11,000 years old.
charlie-lake: In the ice-free corridor between the two ice sheets. Layers c. 12,500–11,000 years ago, with a fluted point c. 12,500 years ago.
great-lakes: Southern Ontario, Michigan, Ohio, western New York. Paleoindian complexes here date to c. 12,900–11,500 years ago; the map date falls on the late Crowfield and Holcombe phases. Dating is mostly geological (shorelines of glacial Lake Algonquin), with few direct dates.
northeast-paleoindian: Paleoindians of New England and the Maritimes, middle phase: c. 12,200–11,600 cal years ago (the early phase 13,000–12,200; Lothrop et al. 2011). Early-phase sites are Debert and Belmont (Nova Scotia), Cliche-Rancourt (Quebec) and Bull Brook (Massachusetts), c. 12,600–12,500 years ago.
western-stemmed: Great Basin and Columbia Plateau: a line of early Americans parallel to Clovis, with stemmed spear points, c. 13,500–8,500 years ago (at Paisley Caves older than Clovis). Lind Coulee: 12,000–11,200 years ago.
channel-islands: The northern Channel Islands of California were then one island, Santarosae, reachable only by boat. Sites of seafaring hunters and fishers with stone crescents date c. 12,200–11,200 years ago.
dalton: Hunter-gatherers of the mid-continent (Missouri, Arkansas, Illinois, Tennessee, Alabama), c. 12,700 to at least 10,400 years ago; Dust Cave (Alabama): 12,600–11,150 years ago. The Sloan site in Arkansas is one of the oldest cemeteries in the Americas.
plainview: Bison hunters of the Southern Plains (Texas, Oklahoma, eastern New Mexico). Begins about the map date (c. 10,200–9,800 radiocarbon years ago); before it — Folsom. Lubbock Lake has a continuous sequence.
cedros: Coastal foragers of Baja California. Shell middens on Cedros Island date to c. 12,240–11,930 and 12,000–9,200 years ago — among the oldest on the Pacific coast of the Americas.
yucatan-caves: The caves near Tulum, now flooded, were dry then. Hoyo Negro yielded the skeleton of a girl, Naia (12,910–12,720 years ago); Chan Hol — skeletons of c. 11,300 and c. 10,000 years ago.
belize-rockshelters: Rockshelters of the Maya Mountains (Mayahak Cab Pek, Saki Tzul) used from c. 10,500 BC: tool making, hunting, river resources. A biface from Mayahak Cab Pek dates to 12,400–12,035 years ago.
panama-paleoindian: Cueva de los Vampiros: a layer with a fluted point, bracketed by dates of c. 13,400–10,200 years ago; near Lake La Yeguada people burned the forest c. 12,900 years ago. Dated only within a bracket.
fishtail: Hunters of guanaco and the last horses and ground sloths, with 'fishtail' spear points: Fell's Cave, Pali Aike, Cueva del Medio, Piedra Museo, Paso Otero 5. The last phase: by the new dates, fishtail points were made c. 12,800–12,100 cal years ago (Waters et al. 2015) — the map date is at the very end. Pay Paso (northern Uruguay): the first occupation ≈ 10,900 radiocarbon years ago (≈ 12,800 cal); Arroyo Seco 2 (Pampas): traces of people already ≈ 14,000–13,000 years ago.
paijan: Hunters, fishers and gatherers of the north coast of Peru, c. 13,000–10,000 years ago, known for long slender stemmed points; the oldest burials in Peru. The Chivateros quarry and the Oquendo workshop (Chillón valley) were stone sources of the Paiján people; Lanning's old scheme (Red Zone — Oquendo — Chivateros) as a sequence of cultures has not been confirmed (Chauchat).
high-andes: The oldest known high-altitude sites in the world, 4,400–4,500 m above sea level: Cuncaicha rockshelter (c. 12,400–11,500 years ago) and the Pucuncho workshop (c. 12,800–11,500). Nearby, in Moquegua, Asana was occupied from ≈ 11,200 years ago.
atacama: Camps by wetlands that existed in the Atacama Desert during a wetter phase, c. 12,800–11,500 years ago.
lindosa: People reached this edge of the Colombian Amazon c. 12,600 years ago; Limoncillos rockshelter is dated 12,470–11,930 years ago. Famous for its rock paintings.
pedra-pintada: Caverna da Pedra Pintada near Monte Alegre: Paleoindian foragers of the tropical forest, c. 13,100–11,400 years ago.
central-brazil: Foragers of the Brazilian savannas: Itaparica tradition tools (unifacial 'limaces'); the first sites around Lagoa Santa appear after c. 12,500 years ago.
bogota: El Abra, Tequendama and Tibitó (where tools lay with mastodon and horse bones). Early layers date to c. 13,800–12,200 years ago, before the map date; later layers are less well dated (dates of the 1970s).
yenisei: The area is drawn from two find spots: the Maina group in the Sayan canyon (layers run without a break until c. 11,500 years ago; nearby is Ui II, c. 12,500 years ago) and Maltat at Derbina (its dates are doubtful); there are no dated finds between them.
shigir: The Shigir Idol, the oldest known wooden sculpture in the world (over 5 m tall, with faces and geometric patterns), was carved c. 12,100 years ago and found in a peat bog near Kirovgrad in 1890.
murray-darling: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Sites: Kow Swamp, Willandra Lakes (Lake Mungo), Snaggy Bend; people lived here through the Ice Age.
se-queensland: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Sites: Kenniff Cave and The Tombs (Carnarvon Range), Wallen Wallen Creek (North Stradbroke Island).
einasleigh: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Sites: Mickey Springs and other rockshelters of the Einasleigh Uplands.
sw-australia: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Sites: Devil's Lair cave, Minim Cove.
arnhem-kakadu: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Sites: Madjedbebe, Nauwalabila, Nawarla Gabarnmang — sequences running without a break from about 50,000 years ago.
kimberley: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Site: Carpenter's Gap rockshelter, occupied from about 45,000 years ago.
tasmania-north: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Tasmania was then being cut off from the mainland by the rising sea. Sites: Parmerpar Meethaner (occupied about 34,000–780 years ago), Warragarra.
ng-highlands: Ancestors of the Papuans. Rockshelters dated close to this time: Kiowa (12,720–11,700 years ago), Nombe, Yuku.
central-ranges: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). The deserts were then as dry as today or drier; people kept to the ranges with water. Pleistocene dates here are few (Puritjarra); Kulpi Mara is dated about 10,900 years ago.
pilbara: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Dates of about 11,300 years ago (Newman, Pilgonaman Creek); the authors consider earlier Pilbara data uncertain.
manus: Ancestors of the Papuans. The island was never joined to New Guinea: people came by sea. Pamwak rockshelter: layer dated about 14,500–10,500 years ago, a human tooth about 11,800 years old; about 13,000 years ago people brought bandicoots and cuscuses to the island.
new-ireland: Ancestors of the Papuans. The island was never joined to New Guinea: people came by sea. Caves Matenkupkum (busiest about 17,000–11,500 years ago), Balof and Panakiwuk; obsidian was brought across the strait from New Britain.
laura: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). No dates exactly at 10,000 BC: the nearest are an engraving at Sandy Creek 1 (at least about 14,900 years old) and layers of about 10,300 years ago.
jomon: Incipient Jōmon, its late stage (c. 16,500–11,500 years ago): the first pottery-using foragers; more than 80 sites are known, from Kyushu to the north of Honshu (Odai Yamamoto I). Kyushu, Shikoku and Honshu were then one landmass.
hokkaido: No reliable dates exactly at 10,000 BC: the nearest are Taisho 3 (Incipient Jōmon pottery, about 15,000–13,700 years ago) and Taisho 6 (from about 11,000 years ago). Sites become much rarer in this cold spell. Hokkaido was then joined to Sakhalin and the mainland.
central-ryukyu: No dates exactly at 10,000 BC: the nearest are Sakitari Cave on Okinawa (layer of about 16,000–13,000 years ago, with shell beads and quartz tools) and pottery on Amami (about 11,000 years ago).
hoabinhian: A technocomplex rather than a single culture: forager groups of caves and river valleys sharing a tradition of pebble tools ("sumatraliths"). The plants they used were wild. The area roughly spans the sites dated close to this time: Con Moong (Vietnam), Tam Hang (Laos), Steep Cliff, Spirit Cave, Lang Kamnan, Moh Khiew (Thailand), Gua Gunung Runtuh (Malaysia); between them there are no dated sites.
niah: Niah Caves: dates of about 12,500–12,100 years ago (Lobang Hangus) and 11,700–11,300 years ago (West Mouth). Borneo was then part of the Sunda landmass, joined to Asia.
gunung-sewu: Caves of the Gunung Sewu hills with long sequences; a burial at Gua Braholo is dated about 12,000–10,500 years ago. Bone tools appear here at about this time.
laili: Laili Cave: layers run from about 44,500 to about 12,000 years ago; the cave was a long-term or seasonal camp.
gebe: Golo Cave: adzes made of shell, about 13,000–11,000 years ago — the oldest in the region.
aru: Probably ancestors of the Papuans. Aru was then part of the Sahul landmass, joined to New Guinea and Australia. Burials at Liang Nabulei Lisa are dated about 12,000–10,000 years ago.
palawan: No dates exactly at 10,000 BC: the nearest at Ille Cave are about 13,800 and 10,700 years ago; the dates from Tabon Cave (about 11,200–9800 years ago) are unreliable. Tools stay the same from the Ice Age into the Holocene.
mindoro: The shell midden at Bubog 1 built up without a break from the Ice Age; the nearest dates are about 13,600 years ago (Bilat Cave) and about 11,000 years ago (Bubog 1).
kurnool: Jwalapuram 9 rockshelter holds the longest microlithic sequence in India, from about 35,000 years ago; its upper dates are about 12,400–11,400 years ago.
balangoda: Microlithic hunter-gatherers of Sri Lanka's rainforests (about 38,000–3000 years ago). Caves Fa-Hien Lena (about 13,000–12,000 years ago), Batadomba-lena (about 39,000–10,000), Kitulgala Beli-lena (about 44,000–8000). Sri Lanka was then joined to India.
sarai-nahar-rai: The only date, 9958–9059 BC, was obtained from bone and is considered unreliable; other Ganga sites (Mahadaha, Damdama) date to the 8th–7th millennium BC.
hotu-belt: Seal hunters' layers start about 9910 BC by the 1950s excavation dates, which are considered unreliable; human bones from Hotu are directly dated 9100–8600 BC; the Mesolithic here begins about 16,000 years ago. Whether these caves belong to the Trialetian culture is disputed.
cyprus-epipalaeolithic: The first known people on Cyprus: foragers who came by sea from the mainland. The Akrotiri Aetokremnos rockshelter was used for a short time, about 300 years, around 11,800 years ago (c. 9800 BC; range 12,100–11,500 years ago). Whether they hunted the island's dwarf hippos is disputed. Deep layers at Vretsia-Roudias in the Troodos mountains are dated to the 11th millennium BC.
santa-maira: The caves of Santa Maira (Alicante) were used without a break c. 13,200–10,200 years ago. Spanish archaeologists call this industry of tiny bladelets the 'microlaminar Epipalaeolithic'; later come geometric microliths.
picareiro: Lapa do Picareiro cave: Late Magdalenian levels dated c. 14,800–11,300 years ago.
backed-points-south: Late Palaeolithic hunters with backed points. On the shores of Lake Federsee (Henauhof Northwest, Bad Buchau-Kappel) there are layers of the last cold spell of the Ice Age; Altwasser Cave in the Swiss Alpstein, 1410 m up, was a hunting camp dated 10,410–9460 BC.
franchthi: Franchthi Cave in the Argolid: people lived here through the last cold spell of the Ice Age (c. 12,900–11,700 years ago); the Lower Mesolithic follows.
antalya: Foragers of the caves near Antalya: at Öküzini the layers run without a break from c. 18,000 years ago into the early Holocene; nearby are Karain cave and the Beldibi and Belbaşı rockshelters (the 'Belbaşı culture' of Russian literature).
mountain-crimea: Shan-Koba culture of the Crimean Mountains (Shan-Koba, Buran-Kaya 3, Zamil-Koba 1), dated c. 14,000–12,700 years ago and later; nearby lived groups of the Swiderian tradition (Buran-Kaya 3 c. 12,700–12,500, Shpan-Koba c. 11,600–11,200 years ago). Later comes the Murzak-Koba culture.
mezmaiskaya: Only one date close to this map: the top of the Epipalaeolithic layer, c. 12,300 years ago (its error range reaches the map date); what came later is unknown.
pymva-shor: Short hunting camps: reindeer and bison bones with cut marks show that people came here twice during the last cold spell of the Ice Age (c. 12,900–11,700 years ago). The northernmost site on this map of Europe.
dnieper-rapids: Among the oldest cemeteries in Europe. Dates on human bone start c. 10,200 BC, within the error of the map date; but these people ate much fish, which makes such dates 300–500 years too old, so the true age may be somewhat younger.
qinghai-lake: Short hunting camps on the shores of Qinghai Lake (about 3,200 m up), c. 15,000–12,000 years ago. The next dated site, Xiadawu (c. 11,300 years ago), lies 450 km to the east.
m1-msa: The Middle Stone Age is a period, not a single culture: hunter-gatherers with Levallois tools and points. Within 135–110 thousand years ago: Klasies River (South Africa), occupied from ≈ 125 ka, human jaws ≈ 119 ka. In East Africa Homo sapiens lived here both before (Herto ≈ 160 ka, Omo Kibish) and after (Panga ya Saidi ≈ 78 ka). Genomes of present-day West Africans carry a trace of an unknown archaic lineage that split off before the Neanderthals; where and when it lived is unknown.
m1-aterian: The Aterian: tools with tanged points, made by early Homo sapiens. The earliest dates come from Ifri n'Ammar (Morocco), ≈ 150–130 thousand years ago. During the last interglacial the Sahara was green, with lakes and savanna; sites are known around the ancient lakes of Egypt's Western Desert (Bir Tarfawi, Bir Sahara, ≈ 140–130 ka).
m1-nubian: The Nubian Complex is a distinctive way of knapping stone (Nubian cores), ≈ 128–74 thousand years ago: the Nile valley and Sodmein Cave near the Red Sea (≈ 119 ka). The same tools occur in Dhofar (Oman, ≈ 107 ka) — a trace of an early dispersal of Homo sapiens out of Africa.
m1-levant-sapiens: Early Homo sapiens outside Africa: Skhul (≈ 119 thousand years ago by thermoluminescence) and Qafzeh (≈ 115–92 ka). Archaic people of the Nesher Ramla type lived nearby; both groups made tools in the same way. Neanderthals reliably appear in the Levant only later, ≈ 70–50 ka.
m1-arabia: During the last interglacial Arabia was green, with lakes. Jebel Faya (UAE): tools ≈ 125 thousand years old resembling East African ones (no bones, so some specialists consider the species unproven). Alathar palaeolake (Nefud): human footprints ≈ 120 ka. The Nefud was settled ≈ 130–75 ka.
m1-nesher-ramla: Nesher Ramla (Israel): human bones of archaic form, ≈ 140–120 thousand years ago — a late Middle Pleistocene group related to the ancestors of Neanderthals; it has no species name. They used the same stone-working technique as Homo sapiens; the authors see this as contact between the two groups. Tabun C1 (≈ 170–90 ka) is seen by some as a Neanderthal, by others as a person of the same type.
m1-india: Patpara (Son valley): Late Acheulean ≈ 140–120 thousand years ago, one of the youngest Acheulean sites in the world; the authors link it to non-modern humans. The Middle Palaeolithic in India begins ≈ 385 ka (Attirampakkam). No human bones of this time are known.
m1-sulawesi: Talepu: stone tools at least 118 thousand years old; at Calio ≈ 1.04 million years. No bones; candidates are Homo erectus, relatives of Homo floresiensis, or Denisovans.
m1-mousterian-europe: Neanderthals of the last interglacial: Krapina (Croatia, ≈ 130–120 thousand years ago), Caours (Somme, France, ≈ 125 ka), Altamura (Apulia, ≈ 172–130 ka). Britain shows almost no trace of people from ≈ 180 to 60 ka. Sicily, Sardinia, Corsica and Crete have no reliable finds of this time. The eastern edge of the zone follows the Dnieper. In the north the zone reaches the Baltic coast and the Western Dvina: there are no finds there (traces were erased by the last glaciation), but niche models show suitable conditions and there is no natural barrier on the plain.
m1-taubachian: The Taubachian: small tools of the Eemian interglacial in Central Europe — Taubach (Thuringia), Neumark-Nord near Halle (≈ 125–120 thousand years ago: hunting of straight-tusked elephants, wooden spears), Kůlna (Czechia), Tata (Hungary). Some researchers think the small size of the tools reflects small pebbles rather than a separate tradition. In the north the zone reaches the Baltic coast. North of Lichtenberg and Lehringen (Lower Saxony, the northernmost Eemian sites of the European Plain) there are no finds: traces were erased or buried by the last glaciation; niche models show conditions suitable for Neanderthals up to southern Scandinavia (Scientific Reports 2024).
m1-mousterian-east: There are almost no directly dated finds from 135–110 thousand years ago here (Shanidar 2 and 4 in Iraq: 'older than 100 ka'). The probability rests on finds before and after, and on the Neanderthals' route from Europe to the Altai, where they lived ≈ 120–110 ka. Anatolia: the long Middle Palaeolithic sequence of Karain Cave near Antalya; ESR dates of its Mousterian layers average 121 ± 27 thousand years (108 ± 23 by another model; Rink et al. 1994).
m1-altai-neanderthals: Denisova Cave: Neanderthals visited it 200–100 thousand years ago, most finds dating to the last interglacial. The Neanderthal woman D5 (≈ 120 ka) and man D17 (≈ 110 ka) belong to related lineages: Neanderthals lived in the Altai for a long time.
m1-altai-denisovans: Denisovans are known at Denisova Cave from bones and DNA in the sediments from 200 to ≈ 50 thousand years ago. The girl 'Denny' (≈ 90 ka) was the daughter of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.
m1-denisovans-east: Denisovans are known mostly from DNA; the bones are a few teeth, jaws and the Harbin skull. Baishiya (Tibet): Denisovan DNA in layers ≈ 100 and ≈ 60 thousand years old; the Xiahe jaw is older than 160 ka. Xuchang (Henan): skulls ≈ 125–105 ka ('Homo juluensis', which may include the Denisovans). Harbin: a skull older than 146 ka, Denisovan by proteins and DNA. Cobra Cave (Laos): a tooth ≈ 164–131 ka. The Zhiren Cave jaw (Guangxi, ≈ 116–106 ka) was once seen as early Homo sapiens; others doubt it. The Penghu Denisovan (off Taiwan) is of unknown age. The edges of the range are conventional.
m1-java: The last known Homo erectus: Ngandong on the Solo River, ≈ 117–108 thousand years ago. The species lived on Java for about 1.5 million years.
m1-flores: The 'hobbits' of Liang Bua cave: bones ≈ 100–60 thousand years ago, tools ≈ 190–50 ka. Their ancestors were on the island ≈ 700 ka (Mata Menge).
m1-luzon: No direct finds from 135–110 thousand years ago: the Callao Cave bones are at least ≈ 50–67 ka old, and the tools and butchered rhinoceros from Kalinga ≈ 709 ka. People lived on the island long before and after.
m1-uninhabited-americas: The first people arrived ≈ 23–16 thousand years ago. The claim that people broke the bones of the Cerutti Mastodon (California, ≈ 130 ka) is rejected by most specialists.
m1-uninhabited-sahul: Australia, Tasmania, New Guinea and the Solomon Islands. The first people arrived ≈ 65–50 thousand years ago. Moyjil (Victoria, ≈ 120 ka): shells and traces of fire without tools; most consider them natural.
m1-uninhabited-japan: The first reliable traces of people date to ≈ 38 thousand years ago; older claims are disputed.
m1-uninhabited-madagascar: Permanent settlement began in the 1st millennium AD; the earliest, disputed traces date to ≈ 10 thousand years ago.
m1-uninhabited-cyprus: The first people arrived ≈ 12 thousand years ago (Akrotiri Aetokremnos).
m1-uninhabited-indian-ocean: The Comoros were settled ≈ 6th–8th centuries AD; the Mascarenes, Seychelles and Chagos only in the 17th–18th centuries. Kerguelen, Crozet, Heard and Christmas Island were found uninhabited in the 17th–19th centuries.
panga-ya-saidi: A cave on the Kenyan coast (near Kilifi), occupied from c. 78,000 years ago. The layers of c. 14,000–1,000 years ago run without a break, but there are no direct dates between c. 14,000 and c. 8,000 years ago.
los-tapiales: A hunters’ camp on a ridge in the Guatemalan highlands (c. 3,100 m, Totonicapán). Main occupation c. 10,700 radiocarbon years ago (c. 12,700 cal); dates on scattered charcoal span 11,170–7,960 radiocarbon years (Gruhn, Bryan and Nance 1977). Obsidian came from three sources 50–75 km away.
capsian-8000: Hunter-gatherers with microliths and shell middens (rammadiyat). The Typical Capsian (c. 9000–6400 BC) began in a small core on the Algerian–Tunisian border: Gafsa, El Mekta, Tébessa, Négrine, Télidjène (Kef Zoura D, c. 10,700–9,300 cal BP). Later, in the Upper Capsian, the culture spread far wider.
west-maghreb: Two areas. The eastern Rif (Morocco): Ifri Oudadane cave, occupied c. 11,000–5,700 cal BP by Epipalaeolithic hunter-gatherers. Western Algeria: the Columnatian (Columnata, Saint-Trivier), main layers of the 8th millennium BC; the map date is at its beginning.
haua-fteah-8000: Haua Fteah cave (Cyrenaica). McBurney's Phase E, the Libyco-Capsian, c. 10,000–7,000 years ago (c. 11,500–7,800 cal BP), following the Eastern Oranian without a break. Excavated in the 1950s; phase boundaries are approximate.
amekni: Amekni rockshelter near Tamanrasset (Hoggar): pottery without farming, the 'Neolithic of Sudanese tradition'. Dates c. 9,650 and c. 8,900 cal BP; a 2025 review places pottery here already in the 11th millennium cal BP.
el-adam: The El Adam phase of the Early Neolithic of the Eastern Sahara (c. 8600–7050 BC): seasonal camps at the Nabta and Bir Kiseiba playas — hunter-gatherers, perhaps the first herders, with the first pottery. People returned here with the rains c. 8500 BC (Kuper & Kröpelin 2006). The second area is Regenfeld in the Great Sand Sea (location approximate): camps of 8000–7000 BC; the map date is at their very beginning.
air-8000: Early pottery of the Aïr massif and the neighbouring Ténéré: Temet, Tagalagal, Adrar Bous 10 (pottery c. 10,300 cal BP). The latest dates, c. 10,200 cal BP, are within the error of the map date; then comes a gap of about a thousand years.
ounjougou: The Bandiagara plateau, Mali. One of the oldest pottery traditions of Africa: phase 1 c. 9400–8400 BC, phase 2 c. 8000–7000 BC (Ravin du Hibou, Damatoumbou). The map date falls between the phases.
early-khartoum: Early Khartoum (c. 8500–5000 BC), at the confluence of the Blue and White Nile (Khartoum, Sarourab, El Khiday) and at the Sixth Cataract (the Sphinx site at Jebel Sabaloka, c. 10,700–10,500 cal BP): fishers and gatherers with early 'wavy line' pottery.
khartoum-variant: The 'Khartoum Variant' (c. 8000–4900 BC), the Nile valley from the Second to the Fourth Cataract: Abka 9, Sai, Wadi el-Arab (c. 8300–6300 BC), El Barga near Kerma (c. 7800–7000 BC).
turkana: Fishers and hunters on the shores of a then much larger Lake Turkana: Nataruk (c. 10,500–9,500 years ago, the site of the oldest known massacre), Lothagam and Kalakoel (bone harpoons), Lowasera on the eastern shore.
buur-heybe: The Buur Heybe inselbergs in southern Somalia. Bardaale industry: Guli Waabayo was used continuously for c. 30,000 years (23 ostrich eggshell dates); Gogoshiis Qabe holds 14 early Holocene burials, the oldest in the Horn of Africa, with grave goods (lesser kudu horns).
eburran-8000: Phase 2 of the Eburran industry (c. 8000–7000 BC, after Ambrose), a very wet period. Sites lie in the Nakuru, Elmenteita and Naivasha basins: Gamble's Cave, Nderit Drift, Enkapune ya Muto.
shum-laka: Shum Laka rockshelter (Grassfields, Cameroon): a microlithic quartz tradition runs without a break for c. 20,000 years; the Holocene layer is c. 10,490–6,210 cal BP. Genomes of people from here (8,000–3,000 years ago) are not ancestral to today's Bantu speakers.
iwo-eleru-8000: A rockshelter in the forests of south-western Nigeria. The red-brown soil layer is dated c. 11,000–6,500 cal BP; canarium nuts c. 11,300 cal BP (Cerasoni et al. 2023). Some dates of the layer are reversed by erosion, so precision is limited.
bosumpra-8000: Hunter-gatherers of the forest margin of Ghana. The first people came in the mid-11th millennium BC, pottery from the start of the 10th millennium BC; the 2008–2011 excavations show the cave was used throughout the Holocene.
matupi-8000: Layers with Later Stone Age microliths run without a visible break from over 40,000 to c. 3,000 years ago (excavations of the 1970s). No direct date at 8000 BC.
hora-8000: The Hora 1 rockshelter was used c. 21,000–8,000 years ago. The nearest direct date to the map date is a cremation c. 9,500 years ago; burials: Hora 1 at 9124–8972 cal BP, Hora 2 at 8170–7960 cal BP.
oakhurst-8000: The Oakhurst industry (with the Albany, Lockshoek and Kuruman industries; c. 12,000–7,000 years ago): non-microlithic tools with many scrapers. DNA of people from Oakhurst cave (the oldest c. 10,000 years old) links them to the ancestors of today’s southern San. Wilton microliths arrive later, c. 8,000 years ago.
pomongwan: Pomongwe cave (Matobo Hills, Zimbabwe): reoccupied after a long gap from c. 10,800 cal BP; the Pomongwan industry belongs to the same non-microlithic tradition as the Oakhurst. Early Wilton is known nearby at Diana's Vow (c. 10,600 years ago).
uninhabited-ice-8000: Covered by an ice sheet (outline approximate, c. 10,000 years ago, after the reconstruction by Dalton et al. 2020). The land was settled step by step as the ice melted.
uninhabited-arctic-archipelago: The islands of the Canadian Arctic Archipelago. The first people — Paleo-Eskimos (Independence I and Pre-Dorset cultures) — will arrive c. 2500 BC.
paleo-arctic: The American Paleo-Arctic tradition: hunters with microblades and wedge-shaped cores (Denali; Akmak and Kobuk at Onion Portage). Transitional period c. 11,000–8,500 years ago.
nw-coast-early: Early sea hunters and fishers of the Northwest Coast. Kilgii Gwaay (Haida Gwaii), c. 10,700 cal BP, with fish and sea-mammal remains; On Your Knees Cave (Prince of Wales Island), Shuká Káa, c. 10,300 cal BP, who ate mostly marine food; Richardson Island, dates 10,500–2,900 cal BP.
old-cordilleran: The Old Cordilleran tradition (Cascade phase): leaf-shaped 'Cascade' points, forest hunters and gatherers of the Northwest. Granite Falls (Washington), 9630–7690 cal BP; Cascadia Cave (Oregon), c. 8810 cal BP and earlier; the lower Fraser; nearby, at The Dalles on the Columbia, the same points.
western-stemmed-8000: The Great Basin and Columbia Plateau: the Western Stemmed Tradition, c. 13,500–8,500 years ago. Sagebrush-bark sandals of the Fort Rock type found here are directly dated to c. 10,400–9,100 years ago — the oldest dated footwear in the world.
channel-islands-8000: California's Northern Channel Islands (Santarosae, breaking up into today's islands as the sea rose): seafaring hunters and fishers of the Paleocoastal tradition, with stone crescents and stemmed points.
cedros-8000: Cedros Island (Baja California): coastal shellfish gatherers. The PAIC-44 shell middens have 13 dates of c. 12,000–9,200 years ago, among the oldest on the Pacific coast of the Americas.
san-dieguito: Southern California and northern Baja California. The San Dieguito complex (scrapers, leaf-shaped and stemmed points) and the early La Jolla (cobble tools, milling stones, shellfish). It is debated whether these are different periods or different activities of the same people; the burial at site SDI-4669 is 9590–9920 cal BP.
plano-cody: The Cody complex (Scottsbluff and Eden points, the Cody knife): bison hunters of the northern and central Great Plains and the Canadian prairies, c. 10,000 years ago.
plano-frederick: The Frederick, Jimmy Allen and Lusk complexes — long points with parallel-oblique flaking: the central Plains, the end of the Paleoindian period.
plano-firstview: The Firstview complex — bison hunters of the Southern High Plains. Lubbock Lake (Texas) has a continuous sequence.
plano-lakehead: The Lakehead complex: sites on the shores of glacial Lake Minong near Thunder Bay (Cummins, Mackenzie), c. 10,500–9,000 cal BP. Quarries of Gunflint Formation taconite; at Cummins, probably cremation of the dead.
golondrina: The Golondrina complex — the first culture of its own on the South Texas Plains, c. 10,000 years ago. Baker Cave has an earth oven with small game and plant remains, c. 9,000 radiocarbon years ago (c. 10,200 cal). Points are found across Texas, Tamaulipas and Coahuila, including the Big Bend.
early-archaic-east: The Early Archaic of the East: corner-notched points (Palmer, Kirk), hunters and nut gatherers in the forests from Florida to the Great Lakes. Hardaway (North Carolina) has Palmer and Kirk layers above the Dalton ones; Rose Island (Tennessee) was first occupied in the second half of the 8th millennium BC and has the bifurcate tradition (c. 7270–6070 BC).
ne-late-paleo: Late Paleoindians of New England and the Maritimes: unfluted points in the dense forests of the early Holocene. The final phase: the Late Paleoindian period is c. 11,600–10,000 cal BP (Lothrop et al. 2011). The Cormier and Nicholas sites (south-western Maine).
el-riego: The El Riego phase (Tehuacán Valley): hunters and gatherers who came together in larger groups in some seasons; the first known burials. AMS dates from Coxcatlán Cave: 9893–7838 cal BP. Before it — the Ajuereado phase.
guila-naquitz: Guilá Naquitz cave (Valley of Oaxaca): the Naquitz phase, c. 10,750–8,670 radiocarbon years ago. Hunters and gatherers; one of the oldest domesticated squashes in the Americas was found here (c. 10,000 years ago).
yucatan-caves-8000: The caves near Tulum, now flooded, were dry then. Chan Hol III, c. 10,000 years ago; Muknal cave has a burial no later than c. 9,600 cal BP.
belize-rockshelters-8000: Rockshelters of the Maya Mountains (Mayahak Cab Pek, Saki Tzul): pre-pottery layers c. 12,500–4,000 years ago; the oldest burials c. 9,600–7,300 cal BP, whose DNA is an early branch of Native Americans distant from today’s Maya.
el-gigante: El Gigante rockshelter (Honduras). The earliest phase is the Esperanza; plant remains span c. 11,000 years: tree fruits (Spondias, avocado) and squash from the very beginning, maize much later.
panama-preceramic-8000: Rockshelters of central Panama (Vampiros-1 and others) were occupied in the early Holocene (c. 10,000–7,000 radiocarbon years ago); unfluted points were made until c. 7,000 years ago. At Lake La Yeguada people burned the forest from c. 11,050 years ago; by c. 8,000 years ago cultivated plants appear (squash, arrowroot).
el-inga: A fishtail-point site on the slopes of the Ilaló volcano near Quito. The dates of the 1960s (9000–4900 radiocarbon years) are considered too young; a new AMS date from Bell's excavations 'agrees with the dates of fishtail points' (PaleoAmerica 2016), but the figure itself is not given in the available text. By the long chronology fishtail points cover the map date; by the short one (c. 12,800–12,100 cal years ago) it is at the very end.
cubilan: Cubilán (sites CU-26 and CU-27, southern highlands of Ecuador): hunters' camps with bifacial points. CU-27: 10,300 ± 170 radiocarbon years (≈ 12,100 cal years ago, about 140 years before the map date) and 10,500 ± 1300 (very imprecise). CU-26 — ≈ 10,400–10,300 cal years ago.
montequinto: A single date, 10,190 ± 90 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,860 cal years ago, about 90 years after the map date): site N2F4-31 Montequinto in the upper Esmeraldas basin, north-west of Quito.
las-vegas-early: Santa Elena Peninsula, Ecuador: the earliest, pre-Las Vegas phase of site 80 (OGSE-80) — 10,840 ± 410, 10,300 ± 240 and 10,510 ± 130 radiocarbon years (≈ 13,800–10,850 cal years ago). Early Las Vegas begins ≈ 11,600 cal years ago (Stothert).
las-vegas: Fishers, hunters and gatherers of the Santa Elena Peninsula, Ecuador: site 80 (OGSE-80) and about 30 other sites. Early Las Vegas ≈ 10,000–8000 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,600–8800 cal years ago), Late Las Vegas ≈ 8000–6600 (≈ 9000–7300 cal years ago); a cemetery at site 80 and early cultivated plants (Stothert).
san-isidro: The pre-ceramic layer of San Isidro on the Popayán plateau: 10,050 ± 100 and 9530 ± 100 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,980–10,580 cal years ago; Aceituno 2015). Grinding stones and palm nuts.
middle-cauca: Sites of the Middle Cauca Valley (Caldas, Risaralda, Quindío: La Pochola, El Antojo, Salento, La Montañita and others): dates from ≈ 12,700 cal years ago (10,619 ± 66 radiocarbon years) through 10,255–10,160 and 9886–9537 cal years ago and on into the middle Holocene (Dikau et al. 2015; p3k14c database). Early foragers of the Andean forests.
guitarrero: Guitarrero Cave (Callejón de Huaylas): textiles of 12,100–11,080 cal years ago (Jolie et al. 2011) — the oldest in South America; wood 10,000 ± 200 and 9860 ± 200 radiocarbon years. Then comes a gap of more than 1300 years (the next dates are ≈ 8500 cal years ago).
atacama-salar: Salar de Atacama and Salar Punta Negra (≈ 2976 m): the Paleoindian settlement of the Atacama, ≈ 12,600–10,200 cal years ago (Grosjean, Núñez & Cartajena 2005). Tuina-1 (10,820 ± 630 radiocarbon years), San Lorenzo (10,400–9960 ≈ 12,300–11,400 cal years ago); points of the Tuina, Fell and stemmed types at Punta Negra.
piuquenes-10000: Alero Los Piuquenes, Río Blanco valley (upper Aconcagua), Chile. The earliest date is 10,115 ± 80 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,700 cal years ago) — about 250–300 years after the map date; there are no earlier dates. Then the shelter is used without a break until ≈ 6700 cal years ago (12 dates).
piuquenes: Alero Los Piuquenes, Río Blanco valley (upper Aconcagua), Chile: 12 dates from 10,115 ± 80 to 5915 ± 185 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,700–6700 cal years ago), among them 8910 ± 70 (≈ 10,000 cal years ago) — on the map date.
puna-jujuy-10000: On the map date — the first, sparse visits: Pintoscayoc 1 (10,720 ± 150 and 10,340 ± 70 radiocarbon years ≈ 12,700 and 12,200 cal years ago, the 'exploration' phase) and Huachichocana III (10,200 ± 420 — a very wide error; 9620 ± 130). Settled occupation comes later (Inca Cueva 4: 9230 ± 70 ≈ 10,400 cal years ago).
puna-jujuy: Early Archaic hunters of the Puna of Jujuy and the Quebrada de Humahuaca. Huachichocana III, layer E3: from 10,200 to 7497 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,900–8300 cal years ago, 'successive occupations'); Inca Cueva 4: 9230 ± 70; Pintoscayoc 1: 9190–9080 ± 50 (≈ 10,350–10,200 cal years ago — settled occupation, a burial) and 7850 ± 110.
huentelauquen-10000: The Huentelauquén complex of the coasts of Norte Chico and Taltal (11,000–8500 years ago; Jackson & Méndez 2005): fishers and gatherers, known for geometric stones. Its beginning is about the map date: the San Ramón 15 red-ochre mine near Taltal is dated 11,800–10,500 cal years ago (≈ 150 years after the map date).
huentelauquen: The Huentelauquén complex of the coasts of Norte Chico and Taltal (11,000–8500 years ago; Jackson & Méndez 2005): fishers and gatherers, known for geometric stones. Near Taltal — the San Ramón 15 red-ochre mine (11,800–10,500 cal years ago) and the Taltal–Paposo rockshelters with Pleistocene–Holocene layers.
umbu-uruguay: The Uruguay phase of the Umbu tradition in the west of Rio Grande do Sul, Uruguay valley: Laranjito 10,985 ± 100 … 9620 ± 110, Milton Almeida 10,810 ± 275, RS-IJ-68 11,555 ± 230 radiocarbon years (≈ 13,400–10,950 cal years ago). Stemmed bifacial points; the tradition lasts many thousands of years.
umbu: The Umbu tradition of southern Brazil (Rio Grande do Sul, Santa Catarina, Paraná, São Paulo): hunter-gatherers with stemmed bifacial points. On the map date: Sangão 8790 ± 40, Capelinha I 8860 and 8795, Caracará 8870 ± 50 radiocarbon years (≈ 9900 cal years ago); Garivaldino 9430–8020, Pilger 8430–8030.
abriense-8000: Sabana de Bogotá. The Abriense lithic tradition (simple flake tools) lasts from the late Pleistocene to the middle Holocene; the finer Tequendamiense technique disappears ≈ 10,000 radiocarbon years ago (≈ 11,500 cal; Aceituno 2015). Tequendama is a continuous sequence of ≈ 13,600–2100 cal years ago, burials ≈ 9000–6500; Checua 8868–8708, Galindo 8722–8375 cal years ago. Direct dates between ≈ 11,200 and 8900 cal years ago are few.
lindosa-8000: By the date model (Morcote-Ríos et al.), phase 1 lasts 12,600–10,000 cal years ago and phase 2 9500–5900: the map date is at the boundary of phases 1 and 2. The interval 10,000–9500 is a boundary of the model, not a proven departure of people (the authors see a departure only 5900–4100 cal years ago). Famous for its rock paintings.
pena-roja: Peña Roja on the middle Caquetá (Colombian Amazon): 9250 ± 140 and 8090 ± 60 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,400 and 9000 cal years ago; Aceituno 2015), seeds 8800 ± 40 and 8730 ± 50. Early cultivated plants: palms, squash, manioc (phytoliths).
atures: The Atures rapids of the Middle Orinoco near Puerto Ayacucho: Provincial 9020 ± 100 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,200 cal years ago); Cerro Gavilán 2 — from 9250 ± 60 to 3440 ± 40 (≈ 10,400–3700 cal years ago; Oliver et al.).
cubilan-chobshi: Cubilán (CU-26: 9100 ± 120 and 9160 ± 100 radiocarbon years ≈ 10,400–10,300 cal years ago; CU-27 is older) and Chobshi Cave near Sígsig, ≈ 60 km away (8615 ± 90 ≈ 9600 cal years ago, and 7535 ± 295).
guaguacanoayacu: A single site on the eastern Andean slopes (Napo): 9850 ± 60 (≈ 11,280 cal years ago) and 8810 ± 60 radiocarbon years (≈ 9900 cal years ago — on the map date).
paijan-8000: The late phase of the Paiján culture (11,200–9600 cal years ago): hunters, fishers and gatherers of the north and central coast of Peru, with long slender stemmed points. Chivateros (Chillón valley) is a Paiján quarry, not a separate culture (Chauchat).
puna-junin: Hunters of vicuña and guanaco in the puna of Junín and Huánuco: Panaulauca (phase 2a, 7050–5910 BC in radiocarbon years ≈ 10,200–8650 cal years ago — the map date is inside), Pachamachay (33 layers without a break; pre-ceramic from at least 8000 BC in radiocarbon years), Lauricocha (Lauricocha I 9525 ± 260 radiocarbon years; burials 8770–8450 cal years ago).
south-central-andes: Early Archaic foragers of the highlands of Arequipa, Moquegua and Tacna and the south-west of the Titicaca basin. Asana (Moquegua): Khituña phase 9820 ± 150 and 8720 ± 120 radiocarbon years (≈ 11,200 and 9700 cal years ago). Toquepala caves: a pre-ceramic layer ≈ 7650 BC in radiocarbon years, paintings of about the same age. Wilamaya Patjxa (Ilave basin, 3925 m): Early Archaic 11,700–9000 cal years ago, burials 9000–8700 years ago, among them a female hunter (Haas et al. 2020). Cuncaicha: the burial of a woman ≈ 9000 years ago.
acha: Acha-2 on the coast of Arica: 8970 ± 255 and 8900 ± 150 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,000 cal years ago) — on the map date. Forerunners of the Chinchorro fishers.
tambillo: Salar de Atacama and the upper Loa. Tambillo 1: 8870 ± 70 radiocarbon years (10,180–9610 cal years ago — on the map date) and 8590 ± 130 (Núñez et al. 2002). An earlier phase of the same basin is the Tuina culture (Tuina-1: 10,820 ± 630; San Lorenzo 10,400–9960 radiocarbon years). After ≈ 8000 radiocarbon years (≈ 8900 cal) comes the 'archaeological silence' of the Atacama basin (until ≈ 5500 cal years ago).
patagonia-early-holocene: Guanaco hunters of the Patagonian steppe and foothills of Santa Cruz and Aysén (the Toldense of Cardich): Cerro Casa de Piedra 7 (11,100–9940 cal years ago), Cueva de las Manos (10,520 cal years ago; paintings from ≈ 7300 BC), El Chueco 1 (10,180–9890), Baño Nuevo 1 (10,870–9460, a burial 10,200–9700), La Martita (8850), Doble Lili (9000–8300). Fell's Cave (Magallanes): above the rockfall 9100 ± 150 and 9030 ± 230 radiocarbon years (≈ 10,200 cal), but 'the chronology of period II is far from clear' (Martin 2022), so the zone does not reach Magallanes.
pay-paso: Pay Paso 1 on the Cuareim river, northern Uruguay: 32 dates, 11,000–8500 radiocarbon years (≈ 12,900–9500 cal years ago; Suárez 2011). Three early components: the first with blade technology, the latest with Pay Paso-type points. Not a fishtail-point culture.
serra-talhada: The Serra Talhada phase in the Serra da Capivara (Piauí): 24 sites of 12,700–8000 years ago; burials and hearths ≈ 11,000–9500 cal years ago (Toca dos Coqueiros burial 11,390–11,170, Paraguaio 10,150–9430); Sítio do Meio, phase Serra Talhada I, ≈ 9400–8100 radiocarbon years. Baixa das Cabaceiras is one of these sites. The disputed Pleistocene layers of Pedra Furada are not part of this map.
central-brazil-8000: Foragers of the Brazilian savannas: the Itaparica tradition (unifacial 'limaces', from ≈ 14,100 cal years ago) and Lagoa Santa (an unchanged industry 12,500–8000 cal years ago). In the middle Holocene large areas of Central Brazil are abandoned (the 'Archaic gap', Araujo et al. 2005).
santa-elina: Santa Elina rockshelter (Mato Grosso): Holocene occupation resumes ≈ 11,000–10,000 cal years ago (hearth F7: 9340 ± 70 radiocarbon years); layer SU-II ≈ 12,000–7000 cal years ago, then continuously 7000–1500 (Vialou et al.). Before that — a gap after ≈ 18,500 years ago.
moxos: Llanos de Moxos (Bolivia): people make 'forest islands' from ≈ 10,850 cal years ago; squash ≈ 10,250 and manioc ≈ 10,350 cal years ago — the oldest cultivation in Amazonia (Lombardo et al. 2020); ≈ 4700 artificial islands.
acacus-tassili-8000: The Tadrart Acacus massif (Libya) and the neighbouring Tassili n'Ajjer plateau (Algeria). The Early Acacus (c. 9200–8000 BC) gives way to the Late Acacus; Takarkori rockshelter was occupied from c. 10,170 cal BP onward without a break; Ti-n Hanakaten — c. 8250–660 BC, hunter-gatherers in the early Holocene; Tin Tartait — pre-pottery layers from c. 9,100 cal BP. One of the oldest pottery traditions of the Sahara.
eastern-sahara-8000: Hunter-gatherers (perhaps already the first herders) of the Eastern Sahara, back with the rains after c. 8500 BC; until c. 7000 BC settlement is still sparse (Kuper & Kröpelin 2006). Local phases: El Adam at Nabta Playa and Bir Kiseiba (c. 11,200–9970 cal BP, first pottery) — the map date is at its end, and the next phase, El Ghorab (7500–7200 BC), may come after a gap; Masara A and C in the Dakhla Oasis (8300–6500 BC); the early Holocene of the Gilf Kebir (8400–4300 BC); Regenfeld in the Great Sand Sea (camps of 8000–7000 BC, with an earlier phase Regenfeld A) — the map date is at their start. The outline is an envelope around these places.
uninhabited-ice-scand-8000: Covered by the Scandinavian ice sheet (outline approximate, c. 10,000 years ago, after the DATED-1 reconstruction, Hughes et al. 2016). The last of this ice melted c. 9700 years ago.
komsa: Komsa: the first settlers of the Arctic coast of Norway (Slettnes on Sørøya, Karlebotn on Varangerfjord), here since c. 11,600–11,000 years ago. The map date is at the boundary of the Early and Middle Mesolithic (c. 8250 BC): later the same people make blades in the 'eastern' technique (Sujala type).
west-scandinavia-8000: Coastal hunters and fishers of western Scandinavia: the Early Mesolithic Fosna (Norway, from the Oslofjord to Nordland) and Hensbacka (Bohuslän, Sweden); sites on the date of the map — Hovland, Hegna, Torkop, Hesthag in Norway, Österöd, Kjuvik, Hanaskede in Sweden. The map date is at the boundary of the Early and Middle Mesolithic: Hensbacka ends c. 10,500 years ago and is followed by the Sandarna culture with microblades; the Norwegian Early Mesolithic lasts until c. 8200 BC. The people stay the same, the stone technique changes.
finland-8000: The first settlers of Finland and the Karelian Isthmus, soon after the ice and the Baltic Ice Lake retreated: quartz tools and slate adzes (in Finnish archaeology — the Suomusjärvi culture, related to Kunda). Sites: Kainuu in the north (from c. 8500–8000 BC), the Antrea fishing net on the Karelian Isthmus (c. 8300 BC). Sujala in Lapland, with blades in the 'eastern' technique, is somewhat later.
kunda: Kunda culture: hunters and fishers of Estonia, Latvia, northern Lithuania and north-western Russia (Pulli near Pärnu — c. 9250–8630 BC, Kunda, Zvejnieki). Lasts until c. 5300 BC, when the Narva culture with pottery replaces it.
butovo: Butovo culture: Mesolithic of the Volga–Oka interfluve (Zolotoruchye, Zamostye 2, Sakhtysh), from the start of the Holocene to c. 5900 BC, when it passes into the Upper Volga Early Neolithic. Its predecessor here was the Resseta culture (its latest dated sites c. 8500 BC). In the west of the interfluve the Ienevo people lived alongside.
ienevo: Ienevo culture: west and centre of the Volga–Oka interfluve (Tver, Moscow, Kaluga regions; the easternmost site is Seltso 3 near Kostroma). Begins c. 11,100–10,800 years ago (Stanovoye 4); the latest sites are of the Boreal period. Butovo people lived here too (Stanovoye 4 has both cultures); Ienevo has its own arrowheads and bone industry.
maglemose: Maglemosian culture: hunters, fishers and gatherers of the North Sea plain and the western Baltic — Denmark, Scania, northern Germany, the northern Netherlands and the eastern part of Doggerland, then dry land (Klosterlund, Duvensee, Friesack, Hagestad, Slochteren). c. 9500/9000–6400 BC, then the Kongemose culture. The old term 'Gudenå culture' (inland sites of Jutland) belongs here. The second area of the culture is Britain (Star Carr type). Typical of the continent are rich peat-bog sites with wood and bone (Duvensee: nut roasting, paddles, decorated bone).
britain-8000: Britain, the second area of the Maglemosian, then still joined to the continent. British archaeologists call this circle the "Early Mesolithic" (Star Carr and Deepcar types; later, in the south-east, the Horsham type with hollow-based points); G. Clark (1932) and some authors today call it Maglemosian. Shared with the continent: broad oblique microliths, tranchet axes, barbed points of bone and antler; typical of Britain: antler "frontlets" made from red deer skulls (Star Carr, 33 of them) and post-built houses (Howick, East Barns, Star Carr). Dozens of sites on the date of the map, from Cornwall and Wales (Nab Head) to Scotland (East Barns, Echline Fields, Cramond, Crathes Warren Field), with Star Carr, Thatcham and Howick. The middle of Doggerland has no finds. Fife Ness is c. 270 years later. Ireland: the first reliable dates (Mount Sandel) are c. 7900 BC, so it is "No data" here.
komornica: Komornica culture: Early Mesolithic of Poland between the Oder and the Bug (Całowanie — c. 8560–8410 and 7530–7320 BC, Komornica). Part of the wider 'Maglemose–Komornica' circle; later comes the Janisławice culture.
beuron-north: Beuronian group of the Early ('first') Mesolithic in northern France and Belgium: segments in the Paris Basin, later the Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt group in Belgium; sites on the date of the map — Meerberg (Belgium), Gennep and Ede (Netherlands). The Tardenoisian with trapezes ('second Mesolithic') comes later. Reinheim on the Saar (late Preboreal) links this area with southern Germany. In the south, as far as Ovno, Pincevent and Noyen (southern Paris Basin).
beuron-south: Beuronian group in southern Germany, Alsace and northern Switzerland, with triangles; the eponym, Beuron, is on the Swabian Alb. Sites on the date of the map: Fohlenhaus (Swabian Alb), Siebenlinden near Rottenburg, Mannlefelsen in Alsace. Lausnitz in Thuringia belongs to the same time.
beuron-bohemia: Beuronian-type Early Mesolithic in northern Bohemia (Bohemian Switzerland): the rockshelters Jezevčí převis and Máselník I are on the date of the map, Okrouhlík I close to it.
sauveterrian: Sauveterrian: Early Mesolithic of southern and south-western France (eponym Sauveterre-la-Lémance, Quercy, Languedoc, Provence, the Rhône valley), the Alps and northern and central Italy (Romagnano III, Isola Santa, Arma dello Stefanin; Fontbrégoua in Provence). c. 9500–6500 BC, followed by the 'second Mesolithic' with trapezes (the Castelnovian in Italy).
corsica-sardinia: The first settlers of Corsica and Sardinia, at this sea level one island: Monte Leone (Bonifacio, from c. 9200 BC), Curacchiaghju (Levie), Strette (Barbaggio) in Corsica, Corbeddu (Oliena) and Su Carroppu (Carbonia) in Sardinia. The Neolithic with Cardial pottery arrives c. 5700 BC.
epigravettian-south-8000: Central and southern Italy and Sicily: industries without geometric microliths, which Italian archaeologists call the 'undifferentiated' Epipalaeolithic or Mesolithic and see as a continuation of the Epigravettian tradition (Grotta Continenza, Grotta di Pozzo, Mora Cavorso, La Porta, Grotta della Madonna at Praia a Mare, Romanelli, Perriere Sottano in Sicily). By this time the north of Italy is Sauveterrian.
ndm: Notched and Denticulated Mesolithic (early phase): both slopes of the Pyrenees, Andorra, Catalonia and the Ebro valley — Balma Margineda (c. 10,400–9550 cal BP), Sota Palou, Zatoya (Navarre), Atxoste and Mendandia (Álava). Cal Sitjo (Barcelona): Mesolithic layers c. 10,200–9100 years ago. Geometric microliths appear c. 8500 cal BP.
ndm-valencia: Notched and Denticulated Mesolithic in Valencia: Tossal de la Roca, Cova Fosca (Castellón; 8880 ± 200 BP = 10,430–9530 cal BP), Benàmer, El Collado. Here it replaces the microlaminar Epipalaeolithic of Santa Maira (until c. 10,500 cal BP). Levantine rock art is not shown as a zone: it has no direct dates.
cantabria-8000: Early Mesolithic of Cantabria, from Asturias to the Basque Country: La Riera, Tito Bustillo, Sotarriza, Ekain. The Azilian has ended by this time; later comes the Asturian culture with its shell middens.
estremadura-8000: Early Mesolithic of Portuguese Estremadura, between Lisbon and Leiria: Toledo, Cabeço do Porto Marinho, Abrigo Grande das Bocas, Vale Frade, Ponta da Vigia. Inland, Fariseu in the Côa valley is of the same time. The shell middens of Muge appear only c. 6400–6200 BC.
nerja-8000: Nerja Cave (Málaga): Mesolithic layers on the date of the map. Shown as a circle around the cave; the rest of Andalusia has no dated finds of this time.
franchthi-8000: Lower Mesolithic of Franchthi Cave (Argolid), c. 10,190–9540 cal BP. The Early Neolithic begins here c. 6800 BC.
theopetra-8000: Theopetra Cave (Thessaly): Mesolithic layers of 10,220–9560 cal BP, with dates both before and after. Shown as a circle around the cave.
adriatic-pupicina: Pupićina Cave (Istria): Mesolithic layers on the date of the map.
adriatic-konispol: Konispol Cave in southern Albania (8900 ± 180 BP = 10,400–9540 cal BP) and Sidari on Corfu (c. 10,190–9610 cal BP). Kryegjata B in Albania is also Mesolithic, but has no exact dating.
kukrek: Kukrek culture: steppe Crimea and its foothills (Kukrek, Vyshenne), the lower Dnieper and the Rapids (Ihren 8: horizons of 8200–7600 BC), the northern Azov coast (Kamyana Mohyla). In the Crimean Mountains — the Murzak-Koba culture (separate zone).
mountain-crimea-8000: Mesolithic of the Crimean Mountains: the Shan-Koba culture gives way to the Murzak-Koba culture (Fatma-Koba, c. 9850–9500 cal BP).
zimovniki: Zimovniki culture: the Seversky Donets basin and the middle Don. Its only reliable radiocarbon date (Plautino-2, c. 9500 BC) is well before the map date; on the date of the map it is placed by pollen and soils (Boreal period). The outline follows the two rivers; the sites themselves are not mapped precisely.
trialetian-8000: Hunter-gatherers of the Caucasus: Kotias Klde in Imereti (8665 ± 65 BP = 9890–9530 cal BP), Kmlo-2 in Armenia (phases of 11,000–10,000 and 9000–8000 BC). Around 6000 BC the Trialetian declines and the Neolithic Shulaveri–Shomutepe culture appears.
central-france-8000: Early ("first") Mesolithic of the Loire valley, Burgundy and the Jura — a transitional belt between the Beuronian group in the north and the Sauveterrian in the south; the sources assign these sites to neither. In the Jura near Lons-le-Saunier (Ruffey-sur-Seille) a Beuronian layer is followed by a Sauveterrian one; the boundaries of the traditions were "permeable". Sites on the date of the map: Les Prés-d'Ingrandes (Vienne), Le Chêne des Fouteaux (Loir-et-Cher), Ouzy (Nièvre), Sur la Noue-la-Lande (Haute-Saône), Ruffey-sur-Seille (Jura), Baume de Montandon (Doubs), Croix du Charnier (near Solutré).
adriatic-montenegro: Montenegro: Crvena Stijena rockshelter — Mesolithic layer, 8870 ± 37 BP = 10,175–9780 cal BP; Seocka pećina by Lake Skadar — 11 dates on bone from 10,670 to 9125 cal BP, two of them on the date of the map. Between the sites lie c. 70 km of mountains (Katunska nahija) without excavated sites of this time.
se-australia-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). The same core-and-scraper tradition as at 10,000 BC. Sites on the date of the map follow one another without gaps: Kow Swamp, Wallpolla and Lake Victoria (Murray), Keilor and Green Gully, Lancefield, Billimina (Grampians), Cloggs Cave, Wyrie Swamp, Koongine Cave, Loggers Shelter (Sydney Basin).
se-queensland-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Kenniff Cave (c. 11,100–9900 cal BP) and Grinding Groove (Carnarvon Range); Wallen Wallen Creek (North Stradbroke Island), Bushrangers Cave and Talgai have dates before and after the date of the map.
einasleigh-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Mickey Springs 34 (c. 10,400–9900 cal BP), Gledswood, Nonda Rock near Ngarrabullgan, the Chillagoe rockshelters (Walkunder Arch).
laura-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Sandy Creek 1 rockshelter: the crust over an engraving is c. 10,500–10,200 cal BP and a layer c. 9500–9000 cal BP — before and after the date of the map.
arnhem-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Nauwalabila, Nawarla Gabarnmang, Ngarradj Warde Djobkeng (Kakadu and Arnhem Land), Garnawala 2 and Nimji (Victoria River district); the Kakadu rockshelters have sequences running without a break from the Pleistocene.
kimberley-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Carpenter's Gap 1 rockshelter: the nearest dates are c. 650 years before the date of the map and c. 1570 years after; at Riwi cave the layers of 9–7 thousand years ago were washed out. There are no dates right at 8000 BC: people probably lived here, but this is not proven.
sw-australia-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Arumvale (c. 10,700–9900 cal BP); Devil's Lair cave has dates just after the date of the map.
pilbara-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Mangenese Gorge 2, Marillana A, Newman (P2055.2) — dates right on the date of the map (c. 10,800–9700 cal BP).
central-ranges-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). The deserts were then as dry as today or drier; people kept to the ranges with water. Puritjarra (Cleland Hills, c. 10,600–9800 cal BP), Kulpi Mara.
nullarbor-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Australians (their languages are unknown). Allen's Cave: hearths dated shortly before and after the date of the map.
tasmania-8000: Ancestors of Aboriginal Tasmanians (their languages are unknown). Tasmania became an island c. 11,000 years ago: by the date of the map people here had been cut off from the mainland for c. 1000 years, and the isolation would last until the 19th century. The culture is still the same as on the mainland ("thumbnail" scrapers); giving up fish and bone tools came only c. 3500 years ago. Sites: Parmerpar Meethaner and Warragarra (Mersey valley), Mannalargenna Cave and Beeton Shelter (Furneaux Islands; people later left them), Carlton Bluff near Hobart (old data: one date from the 1960s, I-323, 8700 ± 200 BP).
ng-highlands-8000: Ancestors of the Papuans. Highland rockshelters: Kiowa, Nombe, Kafiavana, Batari. At Kuk Swamp, about 10,000 years ago, come the first traces of tending plants (taro, bananas); whether this was already farming is debated.
manus-8000: Ancestors of the Papuans. The island was never joined to New Guinea: people came by sea. Pamwak rockshelter: layer C is c. 11,000–7000 years old, a burial c. 10,100 cal BP.
new-ireland-8000: Ancestors of the Papuans. The island was never joined to New Guinea: people came by sea. Caves: Panakiwuk (main layers c. 10,000–8000 years ago), Balof 2 (until c. 7000 years ago; obsidian was brought from New Britain), Matenkupkum (busy until c. 10,000 years ago).
buka-8000: Ancestors of the Papuans. Kilu Cave on Buka Island: people lived here c. 29,000–20,000 years ago, then the cave stood empty for c. 10,000 years; they came back c. 10,400–10,000 cal BP — 100–400 years before the date of the map — and stayed until c. 5400 cal BP. From then on the cave has charred canarium nuts (Wickler 2001).
yangelka: Mesolithic of the eastern slope of the Southern Urals (Yangelka, Mysovaya and other sites excavated by G. N. Matyushin). There are no radiocarbon dates; the age is set by tool types.
novopetrovka: Hunter-gatherers with early pottery and a blade industry in the Amur valley near Konstantinovka; the sites are dated from c. 12,400 to c. 8800 years ago.
sumpanya: Sumpanya IV on Lake Satyginsky Tuman: radiocarbon dates of 11,970 ± 120, 10,910 ± 100 and 10,100 ± 100 BP (the last one c. 12,000–11,300 years ago). The dates were obtained in the 1980s and their link with the finds is not quite clear (Academic History of Yugra, vol. 1, 2024).
kurils: Incipient Neolithic of the Kuril Islands — linear-relief pottery and long barrows on Iturup (Kitovyi 2 and 4), c. 13,000–8500 years ago.
gromatukha-8000: Late stage of the culture; the early pottery of the Zeya and Amur hunter-gatherers lasts here from c. 15,000 to c. 8000 years ago.
ustinovka-8000: Final Palaeolithic of eastern Primorye. The culture spans 16,000–9000 years ago, but no site has a direct date around 8000 BC; Palaeolithic techniques are known in Primorye until c. 8600 years ago.
ust-karenga-8000: Hunter-gatherers of the upper Vitim with pottery; the culture lasts here from c. 16,000 to c. 7500 years ago. 130 km to the north lies Nizhny Idzhir 1 (c. 10,000 years ago).
sumnagin-8000: Mesolithic hunters of Yakutia (c. 12,000–7000 years ago). Shown where the early sites are (Aldan and Middle Lena); in Khatystyr Cave on the Aldan a human dated c. 10,200 years ago was found.
upper-kolyma-8000: Mesolithic of the Kolyma Uplands, c. 11,000–9500 years ago: Burkhala (Sumnagin tradition), Siberdik and Kongo. Siberdik and Kongo are seen either as a separate Siberdik culture (N. N. Dikov) or as a variant of the Sumnagin culture.
duvanny-yar-8000: Only a human skull is known, c. 9800 years ago, without a camp; by its genome — the "Ancient Palaeo-Siberians".
shigir-8000: Hunter-fishers of the eastern slope of the Middle Urals; at Beregovaya 2 in the Gorbunovo bog the Mesolithic layers run without a break c. 11,300–8700 years ago. The Shigir Idol was carved earlier, c. 12,100 years ago.
konda-8000: Hunter-fishers of the taiga Konda: the camp Satyga XVIIa on Lake Satyginsky Tuman and the Mesolithic cemetery Bolshaya Umytya 100; c. 11,000–9000 years ago.
yenisei-8000: The area is drawn from two find spots: Elenev Cave with the Churtas site at the Biryusa bay, and Kokorevo 3; there are no dated finds between them. Churtas is a surface collection from the reservoir shore, Mesolithic by its tool types.
upper-angara-8000: Multi-layer Mesolithic sites on the Angara and the Belaya (Verkholensk Hill, Ust-Belaya, the Badai group, Ulyakha); layers c. 12,900–10,200 and c. 8900–7800 years ago, no direct dates at 8000 BC.
ust-kova-8000: The Ust-Kova site on the lower Angara: a date of 9210 ± 270 BP (c. 11,200–9700 years ago) covers the date of this map.
altai-8000: The area is drawn from two find spots: the foothills of the north-western Altai (Kandabaevo, Komarova Cave) and the Middle Katun (Ust-Sema); there are no dated finds between them. The latest dates are c. 10,300–10,200 years ago (Kandabaevo, Komarova Cave); Early Holocene sites of the Middle Katun (Tytkesken 2, Ust-Sema, Biyke I) have no published dates.
sakhalin-8000: The oldest pottery of Sakhalin — the Puzi 2 site, c. 9800 years ago; the island's Early Neolithic is compared with the Osipovka culture of the Amur.
chessungalane-8000: An open-air site near the Save River. The authors assign horizon II (c. 11,500–8,600 years ago, OSL) to the Oakhurst period; finds are few (208 artefacts) and the dates are of the sediment. Above it is the transition to the Wilton (c. 8,600–6,700 years ago).
ppnb-8000: Early farmers and herders: wheat, barley, pulses, goats and sheep are already domestic or on the way to domestication; houses are rectangular, built of stone. The "Tahunian industry" is an old name for the flint tools of this time.
cypro-ppnb-8000: The first farmers of the island (Shillourokambos, Mylouthkia) brought grain, goats, sheep, pigs and deer from the mainland.
central-anatolia-8000: The first settled villages of the Konya plain and Cappadocia: Aşıklı, Boncuklu, Pınarbaşı (on the shore of Lake Hotamış); obsidian from Göllüdağ travelled as far as the Levant and Cyprus. Farming is only beginning; people live mainly by hunting and gathering at lakes and marshes.
antalya-8000: The last hunter-gatherers of the coast: Öküzini cave and the Beldibi rockshelter (Beldibi Mesolithic). The Mesolithic layers at Beldibi are not dated.
hacilar-8000: The aceramic level at Hacılar is dated by a single old date (Mellaart's excavations, 1960s): c. 10,200–9,400 years ago.
zagros-ppn-8000: Early farmers and herders of the foothills: here, independently of the Levant, the goat (Ganj Dareh) and barley (Chogha Golan) were domesticated. Villages: Asiab, Ganj Dareh, Chogha Golan, Ali Kosh, Nemrik.
bolaghi-8000: Sites of the Bolaghi valley (upper Pulvar), excavated before the Sivand dam was built.
nejd-leptolithic: Hunters with blade tools (the Nejd Leptolithic) on the Dhofar plateau, from the end of the Pleistocene until c. 7,000 years ago; the dates follow the authors' summary (OSL) and have not been checked site by site.
al-rabyah: Al-Rabyah near the Jubbah oasis is the only stratified Epipalaeolithic site of the southern Nefud; its tools resemble the Levantine Epipalaeolithic. A single date of c. 12,250 years ago; its error is not given in the sources available.
hotu-belt-8000: The dates from the 1950s excavations have large errors; the nearest reliable date is c. 10,700 years ago.
sang-e-chakhmaq-8000: Aceramic village; the earliest date (c. 9,900–9,550 years ago) falls just after the date of the map.
obishir-8000: Hunter-gatherers of the foothills in the south of the Fergana Valley: the Obishir 1 and Obishir 5 rockshelters; microliths, shell ornaments; later some of the first barley and wheat in Central Asia.
kurteke-8000: A rockshelter at almost 4,000 m — one of the highest Stone Age sites in Asia; a seasonal hunters' camp. The stone tools are of the same type as at Obishir V.
middle-ganga-8000: Hunter-fishers at the lakes of the Ganga plain: Damdama, Mahadaha, Sarai Nahar Rai; burials inside the camps. The bone dates of these sites are scattered and considered unreliable.
balangoda-8000: The nearest dates are about 11,800 and 8,700 years ago (Fa-Hien Lena); the culture is known from c. 38,000 to c. 3,000 years ago, but there are no direct dates for this time.
shangshan-8000: Early villages with pottery; rice is still wild or at an early stage of domestication.
lijiagou-8000: Microblade hunters who already made pottery, and above them one of the first settled villages of Central China (grinding stones, much pottery).
nanzhuangtou-8000: Nanzhuangtou, Donghulin, Zhuannian — hunter-gatherer sites with early pottery and grinding stones; possibly the first experiments with millet. Nearby at Cishan are pits with millet of the same date (the dating is disputed).
zengpiyan-8000: Zengpiyan cave near Guilin: hunters, fishers and shellfish gatherers with early coarse pottery; occupied c. 12,000–7,000 years ago.
jomon-8000: Initial Jōmon: settled hunters, fishers and gatherers with pottery; the first shell middens.
hokkaido-8000: The Taisho 6 site dates from about 11,000 years ago, with no known break in occupation afterwards. Hokkaido was then joined to Sakhalin and the mainland.
hoabinhian-8000: A technocomplex rather than a single culture: forager groups of caves and river valleys sharing a tradition of pebble tools ("sumatraliths"). The plants they used were wild. The area roughly spans the sites dated close to this time: Con Moong (Vietnam), Tam Hang (Laos), Steep Cliff, Spirit Cave, Lang Kamnan, Moh Khiew (Thailand), Gua Gunung Runtuh (Malaysia), Laang Spean (Cambodia); between them there are no dated sites. In north-eastern Vietnam is the Bac Son variant (tools with ground edges).
niah-8000: Burials in the West Mouth of the cave (seated and flexed), c. 12,000–7,500 years ago.
gunung-sewu-8000: Caves of the Gunung Sewu hills in southern Java: pre-Neolithic layers c. 12,000–4,000 years ago (Braholo, Song Keplek); Gua Mandung and Seropan caves lie in the same karst.
palawan-8000: Ille, Pasimbahan-Magsanib, Tabon; Ille has one of the oldest cremations in Asia (c. 9,500–9,000 years ago).
mindoro-8000: According to the excavators, Bubog 1 was occupied without a break from the Pleistocene until c. 4,000 years ago; there are no dates within ±1,000 years of this map.
gebe-8000: The only date of this time at Golo Cave is considered doubtful by the excavators; the nearest reliable ones are about 11,700 and 7,900 years ago.
laili-8000: Hatu Saur rockshelter near Laleia village: the first phase of occupation c. 10,700–9,000 years ago; in nearby Laili Cave the layers run from about 44,000 to 11,000 years ago.
xianrendong: Xianrendong cave has some of the oldest pottery in the world (c. 20,000 years ago); hunters and gatherers, including of wild rice.
